newsitem.title: RUSSIA: N.Korea envoy hints at Kim's impending succession.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea envoy hints at Kim's impending succession.

text.p: North Korea's envoy in Moscow hinted on Thursday that his country's ruler Kim Jong-il might formally assume the top state positions soon after mourning for his father Kim Il-sung ends on July 8, Itar-Tass news agency said.

"All our people are one in their desire to see Kim Jong-il as supreme leader of party and state as soon as possible," Tass quoted Ambassador Son Song Pil as telling a meeting of members of Russian communist groups and ethnic Koreans living in Moscow.
He gave no details. North Korean embassy officials were not available for comment.
North Korea next week marks the end of a three-year mourning period for Kim Il-sung, the "Great Leader" who ruled his Stalinist state with an iron hand for more than four decades.
Since the death of his father on July 8, 1994, Kim Jong-il, now 55, has established full personal control but the formal top party post and the state presidency have been left vacant.

Western political analysts have said there are no indications that North Korea is preparing a succession ceremony for Kim Jong-il and suggested that the actual dynastic succession was not likely to occur in the next few months.
Moscow is now negotiating a new political treaty with North Korea which would drop the mention of their Cold War alliance and establish more formal long-term relations.

Tass quoted Son as saying that negotiations were advancing successfully and suggesting that Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov could visit Pyongyang later this year when the new pact was ready. He said the invitation had been sent to Primakov.
A Russian foreign ministry spokesman said he could not confirm any definite plans by Primakov to visit North Korea. "I don't think it is on the minister's schedule as of now," the spokesman said.
